terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation; ex and the ablative, with an accusative and infinitive or an indirect question
evidence: Cic. Att. 2.23.1: ex eō colligere poteris quantā occupātiōne distinear
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to gather, conclude, deduce, infer from what precedes (most freq. in Quint.)”. Latin draws the conclusion with a verb where English names it.

evidence: Cic. Fin. 1.22: quō modō efficiātur conclūdāturque ratiō
terms.comment: A term of logic and rhetoric; also “bring to an end, close”.
In logic, what follows from the premises; also the closing part of a speech (Cic. de Or. 2.80).

phrases.latin: numquam ante arbitror tē epistulam meam lēgisse nisi meā manū scrīptam. ex eō colligere poteris quantā occupātiōne distinear.
phrases.english: I don’t think you have ever before read a letter of mine that was not in my own hand. From that you can conclude how busy I am.

sources: Lewis & Short: colligo · Lewis & Short: concludo · Lewis & Short: conclusio
Cic. Att. 2.23.1 and Fin. 1.22 checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
